newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin recovering well, resumes powers in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin recovering well, resumes powers in Russia.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin, delighting doctors by bouncing back from a gruelling quintuple heart bypass, reclaimed his presidential powers on Wednesday and was told he could be back on the tennis court in four months.

"Everything is going quite well and of course it is very gratifying to see this happen because this is a very good sign that his prognosis is excellent," U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey said after visiting the president.

Yeltsin, alert again after his seven-hour operation, signed a decree at 6 a.m. (0300 GMT) which gave him back control of Russia's nuclear arsenal and the other powers which he had delegated to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin for 23 hours.
"He woke up and signed the decree," Yastrzhembsky said. "He surprises doctors with his good state. He feels quite well for this stage."

DeBakey, who pioneered bypass surgery in 1964 and was a consultant at Tuesday's operation in the Cardiology Research Centre in Moscow, said he had warned the 65-year-old president not to take things too fast.
"I said -- You must be very patient, because I know that you want to get going. But I said - You know its very important that you follow the doctors' instructions," DeBakey told CNN television.
But he said Yeltsin could resume light duties in six to eight weeks and resume playing tennis, one of his favourite hobbies before he fell ill four months ago, in three to four months.

"I got the impression he was quite alert and really was feeling good. He expressed that both in his smile and in his statements, and all his expressions indicated he is quite alert and very pleased," DeBakey said.
"Within three or four months he could do almost anything he wants," he said.
Chernomyrdin visited Yeltsin for 15 minutes to pass on many good wishes and report on the state of the nation, the Kremlin said. Yeltsin said he was determined to return to work soon.
Doctors were meeting at the Centre to review Yeltsin's progress and were due to issue a formal bulletin later on Wednesday.
Russian cardiologist Renat Akchurin, who led the operation, said it might be nearly a week before doctors could estimate how quickly and fully Yeltsin would recover.
Yeltsin's prolonged illness has paralysed Russia's post- communist development, damaging Western investor confidence and unleashing a new bout of political infighting in the Kremlin.
The president's friends and foes were waiting to see whether he would take full control of the Kremlin or become a lame duck for the rest of his second term, due to end midway through the year 2000.
Russian markets firmed on Wednesday on news of the operation and Russian debt prices opened stronger in London.
The Kremlin power vacuum is hampering government attempts to resolve a cash-flow crisis which means millions of public and private-sector workers have not been paid for months.
Some Western cardiologists expressed concern at the high number of bypasses performed on Yeltsin, saying that this did not bode well for his chances of avoiding further heart trouble.
But professor George Noon from the Bailey Medical Centre in Houston, who came to Moscow with DeBakey as a consultant, was unconcerned and expected a routine convalescence.
"It is not unusual to see five bypasses," he told Reuters. "The important thing is that the vessels that were diseased were all able to be bypassed and he (Yeltsin) has done very well."
If all goes well Yeltsin could leave the Cardiology Research Centre in 10 days or so.
Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had received invitations to convalesce in Germany and in Slovakia and would decide in due course with his doctors whether to accept.
For a Russian leader to convalesce abroad would mark a sharp departure from Kremlin tradition. But doctors might favour the idea if it prevented Yeltsin from returning to work too soon.
